To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the majority of the Chinese students in this sample reported experiencing some form of psychological distress, and 2) the Chinese participants reported experiencing psychological distress in a manner consistent with the cultural model of the self, which emphasizes the primacy of social relationships and the importance of maintaining harmony.

(a) the prevalence of depression is lower in China than in Western cultures; (b) this difference in depression rates may be related to the fact that Chinese individuals with depressive symptoms tend to express them in somatic ways; and (c) the cultural explanation for this phenomenon may have more to do with the ways in which the self is constructed in China than with the ways in Which the self is constructed elsewhere

1) the Chinese have a lower prevalence of depressive symptoms than do Americans, 2) Chinese individuals with depressive symptoms are more likely to present their distress in the form of physical symptoms (somatization), 3) the tendency to somatize is associated with the extent to which the individual is oriented toward social harmony (i.e., interdependent self-construal)
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cultural construction of self.
the relationship between culture and psychopathology.
the ways that cultural factors contribute to psychological distress and how these processes are manifested.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the somatic complaints of depressed patients in Chinese culture may not be due to the lack of psychological insight or to the lack of the ability to recognize their psychological distress, but rather may be due to a different conceptualization and expression of the same psychological distress.
there are no differences between the two groups in terms of their emotional responses to the film clips.
cultural psychopathology is a field of study in its early stages of development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cultural psychopathology approach is not a simple matter of comparing the incidence of a particular disorder across cultures.
culture shapes the experience and expression, but not the presence of psychological distress.
culture and the self are not only important for understanding psychological processes, but they are also important for understanding psychological distress.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the way we understand depression is culturally specific.
culture matters for the expression of emotional distress.
cultural psychopathology needs to be reconceptualized in order to take account of the cultural constitution of self and the role that it plays in the experience of psychological distress.
